items.stem: What is the oxidation number of oxygen in hydrogen peroxide, H₂O₂?
items.markingKey: Peroxides are an exception: O is −1.

items.stem: Explain why fluorine always has an oxidation number of −1 in its compounds.
items.answer: F is the most electronegative element, so in every bond it attracts the bonding electrons and gains one electron share.
items.markingKey: most electronegative [1]; always takes −1 [1]

items.stem: Explain why oxygen has an oxidation number of +2 in OF₂.
items.answer: F is more electronegative than O and is −1; the sum is zero so O is +2.
items.markingKey: F −1 and more electronegative [1]; sum zero gives +2 [1]

items.stem: Deduce the oxidation number of N in NH₄⁺; Si in SiCl₄.
items.answer: N in NH₄⁺: −3; Si in SiCl₄: +4
items.markingKey: N in NH₄⁺ = −3 [1] Si in SiCl₄ = +4 [1]

items.stem: Deduce the oxidation number of Cr in Cr₂O₇²⁻; C in C₂O₄²⁻; Cl in ClO⁻.
items.answer: Cr in Cr₂O₇²⁻: +6; C in C₂O₄²⁻: +3; Cl in ClO⁻: +1
items.markingKey: Cr in Cr₂O₇²⁻ = +6 [1] C in C₂O₄²⁻ = +3 [1] Cl in ClO⁻ = +1 [1]

items.stem: Jonas is investigating compounds of transition metals and non-metals used in titrations in a research laboratory. (a) Deduce the oxidation number of S in H₂SO₄. (b) Deduce the oxidation number of N in NH₃. (c) State the rules you used for oxygen and for the sum of oxidation numbers in an ion.
items.answer: (a) +6 (b) −3 (c) O is −2 (except peroxides/OF₂); sum equals the charge on the ion.
items.markingKey: (a) +6 [1] (b) −3 [1] (c) O is −2 (except peroxides/OF₂); sum equals the charge on the ion. [2]

items.stem: What is the oxidation number of hydrogen in sodium hydride, NaH?
items.markingKey: In metal hydrides H is −1.

items.stem: What is the oxidation number of Cl in ClO⁻?
items.markingKey: Sum of oxidation numbers = −1: Cl = +1.

items.stem: Explain how the name potassium manganate(VII) shows the oxidation state of manganese.
items.answer: The Roman numeral VII gives the oxidation number of Mn (+7) in the manganate ion MnO₄⁻.
items.markingKey: Roman numeral = oxidation number [1]; Mn +7 in MnO₄⁻ [1]

items.stem: In a test answer, Leila states: "The oxidation number of Cr in Cr₂O₇²⁻ is +12." Explain why this statement is incorrect.
items.answer: The statement is incorrect. 2Cr + 7(−2) = −2 gives 2Cr = +12, so each Cr is +6.
items.markingKey: identifies the error [1]; correct chemistry stated with reason [1]

items.stem: Mohammed writes in a revision note: "The oxidation number of Cr in Cr₂O₇²⁻ is +12." Identify the error in this statement and give the correct version.
items.answer: The statement is incorrect. 2Cr + 7(−2) = −2 gives 2Cr = +12, so each Cr is +6.
items.markingKey: identifies the error [1]; correct chemistry stated with reason [1]

items.stem: Deduce the oxidation number of N in HNO₃; P in PCl₅.
items.answer: N in HNO₃: +5; P in PCl₅: +5
items.markingKey: N in HNO₃ = +5 [1] P in PCl₅ = +5 [1]

items.stem: Deduce the oxidation number of Br in BrO₃⁻; C in CH₄.
items.answer: Br in BrO₃⁻: +5; C in CH₄: −4
items.markingKey: Br in BrO₃⁻ = +5 [1] C in CH₄ = −4 [1]

items.stem: Deduce the oxidation number of Mn in MnO₂; S in H₂SO₄.
items.answer: Mn in MnO₂: +4; S in H₂SO₄: +6
items.markingKey: Mn in MnO₂ = +4 [1] S in H₂SO₄ = +6 [1]

items.stem: Deduce the oxidation number of O in H₂O₂; S in S₄O₆²⁻; Mn in MnO₂. Name one of these species using a Roman numeral where appropriate.
items.answer: O in H₂O₂: −1; S in S₄O₆²⁻: +2.5; Mn in MnO₂: +4
items.markingKey: O in H₂O₂ = −1 [1] S in S₄O₆²⁻ = +2.5 [1] Mn in MnO₂ = +4 [1] name correct [1]

items.stem: Noah is investigating compounds of transition metals and non-metals used in titrations in a university teaching laboratory. (a) Deduce the oxidation number of N in NH₄⁺. (b) Explain, in terms of oxidation number, what happens to manganese when MnO₄⁻ is converted into Mn²⁺.
items.answer: (a) −3 (b) Oxidation number falls from +7 to +2: manganese is reduced (gains 5 electrons).
items.markingKey: (a) −3 [1] (b) Oxidation number falls from +7 to +2: manganese is reduced (gains 5 electrons). [2]

items.stem: A water-treatment chemist in Santiago uses several oxidising agents and needs their oxidation states. (a) Deduce the oxidation number of S in SO₃²⁻. (b) State the rules you used for oxygen and for the sum of oxidation numbers in an ion. (c) Name the compound K₂Cr₂O₇ systematically.
items.answer: (a) +4 (b) O is −2 (except peroxides/OF₂); sum equals the charge on the ion. (c) potassium dichromate(VI)
items.markingKey: (a) +4 [1] (b) O is −2 (except peroxides/OF₂); sum equals the charge on the ion. [2] (c) potassium dichromate(VI) [1]

items.stem: Sofia is investigating compounds of transition metals and non-metals used in titrations in a college laboratory. (a) Deduce the oxidation number of N in NH₄⁺. (b) Deduce the oxidation number of Cr in K₂Cr₂O₇. (c) Explain, in terms of oxidation number, what happens to manganese when MnO₄⁻ is converted into Mn²⁺. (d) Name the compound K₂Cr₂O₇ systematically.
items.answer: (a) −3 (b) +6 (c) Oxidation number falls from +7 to +2: manganese is reduced (gains 5 electrons). (d) potassium dichromate(VI)
items.markingKey: (a) −3 [1] (b) +6 [1] (c) Oxidation number falls from +7 to +2: manganese is reduced (gains 5 electrons). [2] (d) potassium dichromate(VI) [1]

items.stem: In terms of electrons, what is oxidation?
items.answer: loss of electrons
items.markingKey: OIL RIG: oxidation is loss, reduction is gain of electrons.

items.stem: Explain why the reaction Cl₂ + 2NaOH → NaCl + NaClO + H₂O is described as disproportionation.
items.answer: Chlorine (0) is both reduced to −1 in NaCl and oxidised to +1 in NaClO.
items.markingKey: Cl 0 → −1 reduction [1]; 0 → +1 oxidation [1]

items.stem: Explain why the reaction NaOH + HCl → NaCl + H₂O is not a redox reaction.
items.answer: No element changes oxidation number (Na +1, O −2, H +1, Cl −1 throughout).
items.markingKey: no change in oxidation numbers [1]; identifies values [1]

items.stem: For the reaction 4NH₃ + 5O₂ → 4NO + 6H₂O, use oxidation numbers to identify the species oxidised and the species reduced.
items.answer: oxidised: N (−3 → +2); reduced: O (0 → −2)
items.markingKey: oxidised: N (−3 → +2) [1]; reduced: O (0 → −2) [1]

items.stem: For the reaction Cu + 4HNO₃ → Cu(NO₃)₂ + 2NO₂ + 2H₂O, use oxidation numbers to identify the species oxidised and the species reduced. State the oxidising agent and the reducing agent.
items.answer: oxidised: Cu (0 → +2); reduced: N (+5 → +4); oxidising agent HNO₃; reducing agent Cu
items.markingKey: oxidised: Cu (0 → +2) [1]; reduced: N (+5 → +4) [1]; oxidising agent HNO₃, reducing agent Cu [1]

items.stem: Lucas studies the reaction 2Fe³⁺ + 2I⁻ → 2Fe²⁺ + I₂ in a research laboratory. (a) Define oxidation and reduction in terms of electrons. (b) Identify the oxidising agent and the reducing agent. (c) Explain why this is a redox reaction rather than an acid–base reaction.
items.answer: (a) Oxidation: loss of electrons; reduction: gain of electrons. (b) oxidising agent Fe³⁺; reducing agent I⁻ (c) Oxidation numbers change: electrons are transferred (not protons).
items.markingKey: (a) Oxidation: loss of electrons; reduction: gain of electrons. [1] (b) oxidising agent Fe³⁺; reducing agent I⁻ [2] (c) Oxidation numbers change: electrons are transferred (not protons). [1]

items.stem: In terms of oxidation number, what is reduction?
items.answer: a decrease in oxidation number
items.markingKey: Reduction: oxidation number decreases; oxidation: increases.

items.stem: Explain why oxidation and reduction always occur together.
items.answer: Electrons lost by one species must be gained by another; electrons cannot exist freely in solution.
items.markingKey: electrons transferred [1]; must be accepted by another species [1]

items.stem: "Reduction is the loss of electrons." Comment on this statement made by a student, correcting any error.
items.answer: The statement is incorrect. Reduction is gain of electrons (OIL RIG).
items.markingKey: identifies the error [1]; correct chemistry stated with reason [1]

items.stem: Freya writes in a revision note: "Reduction is the loss of electrons." Identify the error in this statement and give the correct version.
items.answer: The statement is incorrect. Reduction is gain of electrons (OIL RIG).
items.markingKey: identifies the error [1]; correct chemistry stated with reason [1]

items.stem: Lina writes in a revision note: "An oxidising agent increases its own oxidation number." Identify the error in this statement and give the correct version.
items.answer: The statement is incorrect. An oxidising agent is reduced, so its oxidation number decreases.
items.markingKey: identifies the error [1]; correct chemistry stated with reason [1]

items.stem: For the reaction Br₂ + SO₂ + 2H₂O → 2HBr + H₂SO₄, use oxidation numbers to identify the species oxidised and the species reduced.
items.answer: oxidised: S (+4 → +6); reduced: Br (0 → −1)
items.markingKey: oxidised: S (+4 → +6) [1]; reduced: Br (0 → −1) [1]

items.markingKey: oxidised: Na (0 → +1) [1]; reduced: Cl (0 → −1) [1]

items.stem: Amara studies the reaction 2Mg + O₂ → 2MgO in a school laboratory. (a) Use oxidation numbers to show which element is oxidised and which is reduced. (b) Identify the oxidising agent and the reducing agent.

items.markingKey: (a) Oxidation: loss of electrons; reduction: gain of electrons. [1] (b) oxidising agent Fe₂O₃; reducing agent CO [2] (c) Cl₂ + 2NaOH → NaCl + NaClO + H₂O; Cl 0 → −1 and 0 → +1. [3]

items.stem: How many electrons appear in the half-equation MnO₄⁻ + 8H⁺ + ?e⁻ → Mn²⁺ + 4H₂O?
items.markingKey: Mn +7 → +2: gains 5 electrons; charge check: −1 + 8 − 5 = +2.

items.stem: Explain why acid must be added in titrations with potassium manganate(VII).
items.answer: H⁺ ions are needed in the reduction half-equation of MnO₄⁻ to Mn²⁺; without enough acid, brown MnO₂ forms instead.
items.markingKey: H⁺ is a reactant [1]; otherwise MnO₂ forms [1]

items.stem: Explain why no indicator is needed in a potassium manganate(VII) titration.
items.answer: MnO₄⁻ is purple and Mn²⁺ almost colourless; at the end-point the first excess drop gives a permanent pale pink colour.
items.markingKey: purple to colourless [1]; first permanent pink at end-point [1]

items.stem: Which overall equation is obtained by combining MnO₄⁻ + 8H⁺ + 5e⁻ → Mn²⁺ + 4H₂O and 2I⁻ → I₂ + 2e⁻?
items.answer: 2MnO₄⁻ + 16H⁺ + 10I⁻ → 2Mn²⁺ + 8H₂O + 5I₂
items.markingKey: Multiply to transfer 10 electrons; cancel: 2MnO₄⁻ + 16H⁺ + 10I⁻ → 2Mn²⁺ + 8H₂O + 5I₂.

items.stem: Construct the overall ionic equation for the reaction of chlorine with sulfur dioxide, using the half-equations Cl₂ + 2e⁻ → 2Cl⁻ and SO₄²⁻ + 4H⁺ + 2e⁻ → SO₂ + 2H₂O.
items.answer: Cl₂ + SO₂ + 2H₂O → 2Cl⁻ + SO₄²⁻ + 4H⁺
items.markingKey: reverse second half-equation (oxidation of sulfur dioxide) [1]; multiply so that 2 electrons are transferred [1]; overall Cl₂ + SO₂ + 2H₂O → 2Cl⁻ + SO₄²⁻ + 4H⁺ [1]

items.stem: Construct the overall ionic equation for the reaction of silver ions with zinc, using the half-equations Ag⁺ + e⁻ → Ag and Zn²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Zn. State the change in oxidation number of the element reduced.
items.answer: 2Ag⁺ + Zn → 2Ag + Zn²⁺
items.markingKey: reverse second half-equation (oxidation of zinc) [1]; multiply so that 2 electrons are transferred [1]; overall 2Ag⁺ + Zn → 2Ag + Zn²⁺ [1] oxidation number change of element reduced stated [1]

items.stem: A pharmaceutical laboratory in Muscat checks a solution of iron(II) ammonium sulfate by titrating 25.0 cm³ portions with 0.0200 mol dm⁻³ K₂Cr₂O₇; the mean titre is 22.40 cm³. (a) Write the half-equation for the oxidation of Fe²⁺. (b) Calculate the concentration of Fe²⁺.
items.answer: (a) Fe²⁺ → Fe³⁺ + e⁻ (b) 0.108 mol dm⁻³

items.stem: In the half-equation Cr₂O₇²⁻ + 14H⁺ + 6e⁻ → 2Cr³⁺ + 7H₂O, what is the change in oxidation number of each chromium atom?

items.stem: Which is the correctly balanced half-equation for the reduction of hydrogen peroxide?

items.stem: Explain how oxidation numbers can be used to balance the equation for a redox reaction.
items.answer: The total increase in oxidation number of the element oxidised must equal the total decrease of the element reduced; coefficients are chosen to make these equal, then other atoms are balanced.
items.markingKey: total increase = total decrease [1]; balance remaining atoms/charges [1]

items.stem: A student in Lagos claims that mnO₄⁻ reacts with Fe²⁺ in a 1 : 1 ratio. Is the student correct? Explain your answer.

items.stem: An industrial process in Nairobi involves the reaction MnO₂ + 4HCl → MnCl₂ + Cl₂ + 2H₂O. (a) Use oxidation numbers to show which element is oxidised and which is reduced. (b) Identify the oxidising agent and the reducing agent. (c) Explain why this is a redox reaction rather than an acid–base reaction.
items.answer: (a) oxidised Cl in HCl (−1 → 0); reduced Mn (+4 → +2) (b) oxidising agent MnO₂; reducing agent HCl (c) Oxidation numbers change: electrons are transferred (not protons).
items.markingKey: (a) oxidised Cl in HCl (−1 → 0); reduced Mn (+4 → +2) [2] (b) oxidising agent MnO₂; reducing agent HCl [2] (c) Oxidation numbers change: electrons are transferred (not protons). [1]

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) What is the mole ratio of MnO₄⁻ to Fe²⁺ in their redox reaction in acid? (b) When combining two half-equations, what must be equal?
items.answer: (a) 1 : 5 (b) the number of electrons lost and gained
items.markingKey: (a) MnO₄⁻ gains 5e⁻; each Fe²⁺ loses 1e⁻. (b) Multiply each half-equation so that electrons cancel.

items.stem: Samuel is constructing overall redox equations from half-equations. Explain why no indicator is needed in a potassium manganate(VII) titration.
items.answer: MnO₄⁻ is purple and Mn²⁺ almost colourless; at the end-point the first excess drop gives a permanent pale pink colour.
items.markingKey: purple to colourless; first permanent pink at end-point [2]

items.stem: Explain your reasoning in each part. (a) Explain why acid must be added in titrations with potassium manganate(VII). (b) Explain why no indicator is needed in a potassium manganate(VII) titration.
items.answer: (a) H⁺ ions are needed in the reduction half-equation of MnO₄⁻ to Mn²⁺; without enough acid, brown MnO₂ forms instead. (b) MnO₄⁻ is purple and Mn²⁺ almost colourless; at the end-point the first excess drop gives a permanent pale pink colour.
items.markingKey: (a) H⁺ is a reactant [1]; otherwise MnO₂ forms [1] (b) purple to colourless [1]; first permanent pink at end-point [1]

items.stem: 25.0 cm³ of a solution of sodium thiosulfate is titrated with 0.0150 mol dm⁻³ I₂, using starch indicator near the end-point. The mean titre is 19.90 cm³. The overall equation is I₂ + 2S₂O₃²⁻ → 2I⁻ + S₄O₆²⁻. Calculate the concentration of S₂O₃²⁻ in the solution.
items.answer: 0.0239 mol dm⁻³

items.stem: Which overall equation is obtained by combining MnO₄⁻ + 8H⁺ + 5e⁻ → Mn²⁺ + 4H₂O and 2Br⁻ → Br₂ + 2e⁻?
items.answer: 2MnO₄⁻ + 16H⁺ + 10Br⁻ → 2Mn²⁺ + 8H₂O + 5Br₂
items.markingKey: Multiply to transfer 10 electrons; cancel: 2MnO₄⁻ + 16H⁺ + 10Br⁻ → 2Mn²⁺ + 8H₂O + 5Br₂.

items.stem: 25.0 cm³ of a solution of sodium ethanedioate is titrated with 0.0150 mol dm⁻³ KMnO₄ in the presence of dilute sulfuric acid. The mean titre is 24.35 cm³. The overall equation is 2MnO₄⁻ + 16H⁺ + 5C₂O₄²⁻ → 2Mn²⁺ + 8H₂O + 10CO₂. Calculate the concentration of C₂O₄²⁻ in the solution.
items.answer: 0.0365 mol dm⁻³

items.stem: A pharmaceutical laboratory in Seoul checks a solution of sodium ethanedioate by titrating 25.0 cm³ portions with 0.0200 mol dm⁻³ KMnO₄; the mean titre is 24.10 cm³. (a) Write the half-equation for the oxidation of C₂O₄²⁻. (b) Calculate the concentration of C₂O₄²⁻.
items.answer: (a) C₂O₄²⁻ → 2CO₂ + 2e⁻ (b) 0.0482 mol dm⁻³

items.stem: Omar determines the concentration of sodium ethanedioate by titration with 0.0200 mol dm⁻³ KMnO₄. 25.0 cm³ of the solution requires 20.80 cm³. (a) Write the half-equation for the reduction of the oxidising agent. (b) Construct the overall ionic equation. (c) Calculate the concentration of C₂O₄²⁻.
items.answer: (a) MnO₄⁻ + 8H⁺ + 5e⁻ → Mn²⁺ + 4H₂O (b) 2MnO₄⁻ + 16H⁺ + 5C₂O₄²⁻ → 2Mn²⁺ + 8H₂O + 10CO₂ (c) 0.0416 mol dm⁻³

items.stem: What is the oxidation number of any element in its uncombined state?
items.markingKey: e.g. Cl₂, Fe, O₂, S₈ all have oxidation number 0.

items.stem: Mei is assigning oxidation numbers to elements in a set of compounds. Explain why fluorine always has an oxidation number of −1 in its compounds.
items.answer: F is the most electronegative element, so in every bond it attracts the bonding electrons and gains one electron share.
items.markingKey: most electronegative; always takes −1 [2]

items.stem: Samuel is assigning oxidation numbers to elements in a set of compounds. Explain why oxygen has an oxidation number of +2 in OF₂.
items.answer: F is more electronegative than O and is −1; the sum is zero so O is +2.
items.markingKey: F −1 and more electronegative; sum zero gives +2 [2]

items.stem: Deduce the oxidation number of Mn in MnO₂; Cl in ClO⁻.
items.answer: Mn in MnO₂: +4; Cl in ClO⁻: +1
items.markingKey: Mn in MnO₂ = +4 [1] Cl in ClO⁻ = +1 [1]

items.stem: Deduce the oxidation number of N in HNO₃; P in P₄O₁₀; H in NaH.
items.answer: N in HNO₃: +5; P in P₄O₁₀: +5; H in NaH: −1
items.markingKey: N in HNO₃ = +5 [1] P in P₄O₁₀ = +5 [1] H in NaH = −1 [1]

items.stem: Ravi is investigating compounds of transition metals and non-metals used in titrations in a college laboratory. (a) Deduce the oxidation number of S in H₂SO₄. (b) Deduce the oxidation number of Cr in Cr₂O₇²⁻. (c) Explain, in terms of oxidation number, what happens to manganese when MnO₄⁻ is converted into Mn²⁺.
items.answer: (a) +6 (b) +6 (c) Oxidation number falls from +7 to +2: manganese is reduced (gains 5 electrons).
items.markingKey: (a) +6 [1] (b) +6 [1] (c) Oxidation number falls from +7 to +2: manganese is reduced (gains 5 electrons). [2]

items.stem: What is disproportionation?
options: a reaction in which the same element is simultaneously oxidised and reduced
a reaction in which two elements swap places
items.answer: a reaction in which the same element is simultaneously oxidised and reduced
items.markingKey: e.g. Cl₂ + 2NaOH → NaCl + NaClO + H₂O.

items.stem: Explain, using oxidation numbers, why the reaction Cl₂ + H₂O → HCl + HClO is an example of disproportionation.
items.answer: The oxidation number of chlorine changes from 0 to −1 (in HCl) (reduction) and from 0 to +1 (in HClO) (oxidation): the same element is both oxidised and reduced.
items.markingKey: oxidation numbers correct [1]; same element both oxidised and reduced [1]

items.stem: Ravi is analysing redox reactions met in AS chemistry. (a) Explain why oxidation and reduction always occur together. (b) Explain why the reaction NaOH + HCl → NaCl + H₂O is not a redox reaction.
items.answer: (a) Electrons lost by one species must be gained by another; electrons cannot exist freely in solution. (b) No element changes oxidation number (Na +1, O −2, H +1, Cl −1 throughout).
items.markingKey: (a) electrons transferred; must be accepted by another species [2] (b) no change in oxidation numbers; identifies values [2]

items.stem: For the reaction Cu + 4HNO₃ → Cu(NO₃)₂ + 2NO₂ + 2H₂O, use oxidation numbers to identify the species oxidised and the species reduced.
items.answer: oxidised: Cu (0 → +2); reduced: N (+5 → +4)
items.markingKey: oxidised: Cu (0 → +2) [1]; reduced: N (+5 → +4) [1]

items.stem: An industrial process in Toronto involves the reaction 2HBr + H₂SO₄ → Br₂ + SO₂ + 2H₂O. (a) Define oxidation and reduction in terms of electrons. (b) Identify the oxidising agent and the reducing agent.
items.answer: (a) Oxidation: loss of electrons; reduction: gain of electrons. (b) oxidising agent H₂SO₄; reducing agent HBr
items.markingKey: (a) Oxidation: loss of electrons; reduction: gain of electrons. [1] (b) oxidising agent H₂SO₄; reducing agent HBr [2]

items.stem: Zara studies the reaction 2HBr + H₂SO₄ → Br₂ + SO₂ + 2H₂O in a research laboratory. (a) Define oxidation and reduction in terms of electrons. (b) Explain why this is a redox reaction rather than an acid–base reaction. (c) Write the equation for the reaction of chlorine with cold aqueous sodium hydroxide and explain why it is a disproportionation.
items.answer: (a) Oxidation: loss of electrons; reduction: gain of electrons. (b) Oxidation numbers change: electrons are transferred (not protons). (c) Cl₂ + 2NaOH → NaCl + NaClO + H₂O; Cl 0 → −1 and 0 → +1.
items.markingKey: (a) Oxidation: loss of electrons; reduction: gain of electrons. [1] (b) Oxidation numbers change: electrons are transferred (not protons). [1] (c) Cl₂ + 2NaOH → NaCl + NaClO + H₂O; Cl 0 → −1 and 0 → +1. [3]

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) How many electrons appear in the half-equation MnO₄⁻ + 8H⁺ + ?e⁻ → Mn²⁺ + 4H₂O? (b) State what is added to balance oxygen atoms in a half-equation in acidic solution.
items.answer: (a) 5 (b) Water molecules (H₂O), then H⁺ ions to balance hydrogen.
items.markingKey: (a) Mn +7 → +2: gains 5 electrons; charge check: −1 + 8 − 5 = +2. (b) [1]

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) Explain why no indicator is needed in a potassium manganate(VII) titration. (b) Explain how oxidation numbers can be used to balance the equation for a redox reaction.
items.answer: (a) MnO₄⁻ is purple and Mn²⁺ almost colourless; at the end-point the first excess drop gives a permanent pale pink colour. (b) The total increase in oxidation number of the element oxidised must equal the total decrease of the element reduced; coefficients are chosen to make these equal, then other atoms are balanced.
items.markingKey: (a) purple to colourless [1]; first permanent pink at end-point [1] (b) total increase = total decrease [1]; balance remaining atoms/charges [1]

items.stem: "The half-equation Fe²⁺ → Fe³⁺ shows reduction." Comment on this statement made by a student, correcting any error.
items.answer: The statement is incorrect. Fe²⁺ → Fe³⁺ + e⁻ is oxidation: electrons are lost.
items.markingKey: identifies the error [1]; correct chemistry stated with reason [1]

items.stem: 25.0 cm³ of a solution of iron(II) ammonium sulfate is titrated with 0.0100 mol dm⁻³ K₂Cr₂O₇ in the presence of dilute sulfuric acid. The mean titre is 24.35 cm³. The overall equation is Cr₂O₇²⁻ + 14H⁺ + 6Fe²⁺ → 2Cr³⁺ + 7H₂O + 6Fe³⁺. Calculate the concentration of Fe²⁺ in the solution.
items.answer: 0.0584 mol dm⁻³

items.stem: Which overall equation is obtained by combining Ag⁺ + e⁻ → Ag and Zn → Zn²⁺ + 2e⁻?
items.answer: 2Ag⁺ + Zn → 2Ag + Zn²⁺
items.markingKey: Multiply to transfer 2 electrons; cancel: 2Ag⁺ + Zn → 2Ag + Zn²⁺.

items.stem: 25.0 cm³ of a solution of hydrogen peroxide is titrated with 0.0150 mol dm⁻³ KMnO₄ in the presence of dilute sulfuric acid. The mean titre is 24.35 cm³. The overall equation is 2MnO₄⁻ + 6H⁺ + 5H₂O₂ → 2Mn²⁺ + 8H₂O + 5O₂. Calculate the concentration of H₂O₂ in the solution.
items.answer: 0.0365 mol dm⁻³

items.stem: A pharmaceutical laboratory in Lima checks a solution of sodium ethanedioate by titrating 25.0 cm³ portions with 0.0200 mol dm⁻³ KMnO₄; the mean titre is 22.40 cm³. (a) Write the half-equation for the oxidation of C₂O₄²⁻. (b) Calculate the concentration of C₂O₄²⁻.
items.answer: (a) C₂O₄²⁻ → 2CO₂ + 2e⁻ (b) 0.0448 mol dm⁻³

items.stem: Ines determines the concentration of sodium ethanedioate by titration with 0.0200 mol dm⁻³ KMnO₄. 25.0 cm³ of the solution requires 24.10 cm³. (a) Calculate the concentration of C₂O₄²⁻. (b) Describe the colour change at the end-point. (c) Explain why the titration is carried out in excess dilute sulfuric acid rather than hydrochloric acid.
items.answer: (a) 0.0482 mol dm⁻³ (b) Colourless (pale) to first permanent pale pink (c) H⁺ needed; HCl would be oxidised by the strong oxidant to Cl₂, giving a larger titre.
items.markingKey: (a) n(ox) = 0.000482; × 5/2; ÷ 0.0250 [3] (b) Colourless (pale) to first permanent pale pink [1] (c) H⁺ needed; HCl would be oxidised by the strong oxidant to Cl₂, giving a larger titre. [2]
